Experiments on VIGORv2 show that SDU-G2A improves BEV land-cover estimation, reduces radial prediction errors, and achieves stronger geospatial correspondence and aerial-feature distributional realism than representative G2A baselines. These results indicate that self-derived land-cover uncertainty can bridge cross-view semantic footprint inference and reliable remote-sensing image synthesis from accessible street-level observations.

title: Object-Based Reconstruction of Mining-Associated Water Body Lifecycles from Multisource Satellite Time Series
summary: Mining-associated water bodies are typically mapped as independent annual patches, obscuring their formation, transformation and continuity over time. Changes in visible water therefore need to be distinguished from changes in water body identity and surface state. Here, we develop an object-based, interval-aware framework to reconstruct water body lifecycles across seven domains in the Huainan and Huaibei coalfields, China, separating persistent identity from geometry and surface state. The framework integrates Landsat, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope and RapidEye imagery with contextual evidence to interpret changes and constrain event timing. Across these domains, the screened visible water area increased by 853.0 ha between the 2015–2017 and 2022–2024 epochs, comprising 1758.4 ha of gain and 905.4 ha of loss. The case histories documented continuity under photovoltaic cover and engineered subdivision, as well as terrestrial surface conversion with an unresolved termination status. In the examined cases, the changes in area and component overlap did not uniquely identify lifecycle events without temporal and spatial context evidence. Dense image sequences documented the early development and expansion of individual water bodies and bounded coalescence events. An independent blinded review reproduced 94.4% (17/18) of identity-relation decisions and all endpoint decisions in the original review sample. By distinguishing object continuity from visible water change, the framework complements area-based monitoring by providing evidence of water body lifecycle processes.

title: Dual Category-Guided Spatial Mamba Network for Remote Sensing Semantic Segmentation
summary: With the rapid development of aerospace technology, remote sensing images contain increasingly rich feature information, while large variations in object scales and imbalanced category distributions pose great challenges to remote sensing semantic segmentation. Current mainstream methods often rely on attention mechanisms for global modeling, yet they tend to over-average features, making it difficult to capture minority categories and preserve fine-grained details. To address these limitations, we propose a Dual Category-Guided Spatial Mamba Network (DGSMNet) that combines dual category guidance with a spatial Mamba mechanism. Specifically, a Dual-Stage Category Guidance (DSCG) module is designed to extract class information via wavelet transforms and guide feature learning, ensuring proportional representation of all categories across channels and enabling the model to learn underrepresented classes. In addition, a Spatial Mamba (SPM) module is introduced to enhance long-range modeling while retaining sensitivity to local details. By integrating DSCG and SPM, the proposed DGSMNet improves category-aware representation and spatial modeling on the evaluated benchmarks. Extensive experiments on the ISPRS Vaihingen and Potsdam datasets demonstrate that DGSMNet achieves competitive performance among the compared methods.

title: Robust Satellite Techniques for Detecting and Monitoring Icebergs by Sentinel-2 Data
summary: In recent decades, the sharp rise in global temperatures has accelerated the melting of the polar ice caps, causing icebergs to break off and subsequently drift across the sea surface. At the same time, the increase in navigable areas in the Arctic region has led to a continued growth in maritime traffic at higher latitudes, resulting in a consequent increase in the risk of iceberg–ship collisions. In this context, it is particularly important to provide vessels at sea with timely and up-to-date information on the presence of icebergs along routes in mid- and high-latitude waters. Given this challenge, this paper presents, for the first time, the Robust Satellite Techniques (RST) methodology employed at the global level to perform iceberg detection using imagery acquired only in the B3 band (centred at 560 nm) by the Sentinel-2 (S2) constellation. A test performed near Greenland (in September 2016) and in the Labrador Sea (in August 2021), showed that, in comparison with traditional fixed-threshold methods, this approach (easily implementable in the Google Earth Engine cloud platform) demonstrated: (a) very high sensitivity by doubling the number of detected icebergs (including the smaller ones); (b) high reliability with an overall false positive below 20% that becomes zero when other objects that may pose a hazard to navigation (e.g., dark ships, shallow reefs, etc.) are also considered.

title: Kernel-Driven Model Correction of Thermal Directionality: Pixel-Level Analysis Using Airborne Multi-Angular Observations
summary: Directional anisotropy (DA) in thermal infrared (TIR) remote sensing introduces significant variability in land surface temperature (LST) retrievals, particularly in high-resolution observations. This study presents the empirical pixel-level modelling of DA, by using multi-angular airborne data from the NETSense campaign over an agricultural area near Grosseto, Italy. Six kernel-driven models (KDMs) are evaluated for their ability to fit directional effects, with the Vinnikov–Roujean–Lagouarde (Vinnikov–RL) model achieving the highest accuracy (RMSE = 1.07 K). At 40 m resolution, modelled directional effects reach median deviations of +1.80 K at the hotspot position, −2.03 K opposite to the Sun, and −1.37 K perpendicular to the solar principal plane, with extremes up to ±6 K, highlighting their operational significance for missions such as LSTM, TRISHNA, and SBG. To improve operational feasibility, two simplified models—adapted RL (RLa) and Vinnikov–RLa—are introduced, leveraging a consistent inverse relationship between hotspot magnitude and width to reduce parameter complexity via a power-law formulation. The analysis reveals that directional effects vary with spatial resolution and are influenced by canopy structure and solar geometry, while biophysical parameters alone are insufficient for coefficient estimation. Validation using an independent flight day confirms the robustness of the simplified models under different acquisition geometries, surface types, and geophysical conditions. A tiered model strategy is proposed for future satellite missions, recommending model selection based on day or night observations and data availability. These findings support the integration of directional correction into operational pipelines, enabling consistent and accurate LST products across platforms, resolutions, and observation conditions.

title: Migratory Bird Identification and Density Prediction Based on Weather Radar Products and Weather Forecast Information
summary: Bird activity levels present an increasing trend in China. Bird strike risks for the aviation industry are positively correlated with bird activity. Migratory birds pose greater threats to airplanes due to their broader distribution and larger mass. A reliable broad-area surveillance solution for migratory birds is critical for bird strike warning and prevention. This paper introduces a broad-area migratory bird identification model based on weather radar systems. A customized feature space and a sample-separation optimization strategy are proposed for more accurate identification of bird targets in weather radar resolution volumes. A new bird density calculation model is proposed to accommodate nonuniform bird distributions and provide a more reasonable bird quantity interpretation. The relevance between bird density and weather parameters is modeled by specific data sampling and a numerical regression model. Weather radar data files from two stations in China are used to verify the effectiveness of the proposed method. Results indicate that the bird identification model could provide reasonable bird surveillance information, and the density prediction models present good consistency with existing datasets. Differences among radar stations and seasons prove the necessity of building individual bird density prediction models. Identification and prediction models are expected to be further optimized with more data support and cross-validation information. Quantitative and qualitative prediction products provide valuable references for bird strike prediction and prevention.

title: Multi-Source Remote Sensing for Mangrove Mapping in South China: Sensor-Configuration Responses and Cross-Regional Model Applicability
summary: Mangrove mapping increasingly integrates multisource remote sensing, yet the geographically transferable value of additional sensors remains uncertain. This study evaluated Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery, Sentinel-1 and GF-3 SAR, GF-5 AHSI hyperspectral observations, terrain variables, and sensor-independent coastal-context information across five coastal regions of southern China. Five nested feature configurations (D1–D5) were tested with Random Forest, XGBoost, DeepLabV3, and SegFormer under true leave-one-study-area-out validation on 349,898 common 10 m coordinates; deep models were replicated across three random seeds. Model-averaged F1-scores were 0.9025, 0.9031, 0.9123, 0.9134, and 0.9220 for D1–D5, respectively, but differences were not statistically supported across held-out regions (Friedman χ2 = 0.48, p = 0.9754). Sentinel-1, GF-3, and their interaction showed small, geographically inconsistent contrasts. GF-5 effects were model- and preprocessing-dependent, and cross-scene normalization altered performance in contrasting directions. Gain and grouped-permutation analyses indicated model-specific predictor use and sensitivity rather than independent sensor contribution. Overall, multisource benefits depended on sensor configuration, model representation, geographic domain, and preprocessing conditions, supporting context-specific sensor selection and geographically independent validation.

title: Systematic Divergence Between NDVI-Based and Energy-Balance Water-Stress Classifications in Sparse Hyper-Arid Olive Orchards: A Two-Decade Landsat–METRIC Evaporative CWSI Assessment
summary: Water stress in olive orchards is often mapped from the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), although in sparse orchards NDVI also reflects fractional cover and bare soil. We compared an NDVI-based classification with a METRIC-derived evaporative Crop Water Stress Index (CWSIET=1−ETa/ETo) over hyper-arid, groundwater-irrigated olive orchards of La Yarada–Los Palos (Peru), using Landsat 5/8/9 imagery from eighteen austral summers (2006–2026). Both classifications rely on operational thresholds that were not physiologically calibrated for olive: the NDVI ranges were defined from field-observed canopy condition, and the CWSIET classes are equal-width bins of the reference-normalized evaporative deficit. NDVI placed most of the cropland in severe-to-extreme classes and CWSIET mainly in mild-to-moderate classes (medians 0.26–0.41); NDVI was more severe over 89% of the cropland. The divergence grew as cover decreased, persisted at native thermal resolution and was reproduced by surface temperature, although both continuous indices correlated (r=−0.61). Without in situ physiological or flux measurements, these results establish a disagreement between indicators, not which of them matches plant water status. The cropland expanded fourfold (98 to 356 km2) with no trend in mean evapotranspiration or CWSIET. NDVI-based stress maps should be interpreted with caution in sparse orchards and combined with energy-balance, meteorological or field information.

title: Evaluation of L-Band SMAP Scatterometer Tropical Cyclone Wind Retrieval Using UHR σ° Measurements
summary: Tropical cyclones pose a significant hazard to coastal populations and shipping infrastructure. By helping provide timely warnings, ocean scatterometers can mitigate this threat with ocean wind estimates. In this study, the Soil Moisture Active/Passive (SMAP) mission is used to evaluate the effectiveness of wind estimates using L-band scatterometry for tropical cyclones. Standard-resolution SMAP scatterometer normalized radar backscatter (σ∘) measurements are enhanced to a much finer spatial resolution using the Ultra-High Resolution (UHR) algorithm, from which high-to-severe winds are estimated. The influence of σ∘ polarization (Horizontal HH-, Vertical VV-, and Cross X-pol) on wind estimates at high-to-severe winds is assessed. In this study, a new wind model is created with tropical cyclone Best-Track data, SMAP σ∘ measurements, and Numerical Weather Prediction winds. The Best-Track-derived wind model and SMAP UHR σ∘ measurements are used to create a Geophysical Model Function (GMF), and wind retrieval is performed. Analysis of wind retrieval estimates demonstrates that the HH- and VV-pol σ∘ tend to saturate at high-to-severe winds while X-pol measurements do not. Retrieved UHR winds generally align with the Best-Track derived wind model, although the errors can exceed desirable tolerances for speed and direction (i.e., less than 10% m/s and 20° Root Mean Square Error). Ultimately, these results suggest that L-band scatterometer wind estimation has potential for tropical cyclone monitoring by increasing the SNR of X-pol σ∘ measurements.

title: A Spatial-Domain Crest-Line Tracking Method for Swell-Based Shallow-Water Bathymetry Retrieval from Sentinel-1 SAR Imagery
summary: Shallow-water bathymetry is essential for coastal dynamics, navigation, engineering, and marine-resource management, especially where in situ observations are sparse. This study proposes a wave-stripe-based method for shallow-water bathymetric retrieval from Sentinel-1A VV-polarized SAR imagery. After texture-preserving denoising, multidirectional Gabor enhancement, K-means segmentation, and skeleton tracking, wave-crest centerlines are extracted and local wavelengths are measured as the normal spacing between adjacent crest lines. The dominant wave period is estimated from deep-water wavelengths, and water depth is retrieved using the linear wave dispersion relation. The method was evaluated using five Sentinel-1 acquisitions, with SAR-derived representative wave periods ranging from 12.45 to 14.96 s. Based on the mean retrieval performance across the five acquisitions, the 0–20 m depth range yielded an RMSE of 3.87 m, an MAE of 3.56 m, and r = 0.95, while the corresponding values for 0–50 m were 6.06 m, 5.02 m, and 0.97, respectively. The most stable performance occurred within the 5–20 m depth range. The method reduces fixed-window spectral averaging and improves the representation of local wavelength variability, supporting rapid bathymetric mapping along open-coast environments with clear swell-induced wave stripes, relatively gentle bathymetric slopes, and limited field observations.

title: HFER-SAM: Boundary-Aware Segment Anything Model via High-Frequency Enhanced and Residual Injection for Building Extraction
summary: Automatic building extraction from high-resolution remote sensing imagery is vital for urban applications. Although the Segment Anything Model (SAM) offers powerful semantic capabilities, its direct application faces severe challenges. The inherent low-pass filtering of Vision Transformers typically causes blurred building edges, distorted right angles, and severe adhesion among dense clusters. To address these bottlenecks, we propose a Boundary-Aware Segment Anything Model via High-Frequency Enhanced and Residual Injection (HFER-SAM). First, a Multi-scale Semantic Adaptation Module (MSAM) uses domain adapters and coordinate attention to recover spatial priors for precise domain alignment. Second, a High-Frequency Residual Injection Module (HFRIM) employs a lightweight CNN to extract roof textures and edge gradients. These are injected as residual terms into the semantic stream to explicitly sharpen physical boundaries. Finally, a Boundary-Constrained Dual-Task Head (BC-DTH) utilizes morphological supervision to sever erroneous connections between adjacent buildings and resolve target adhesion. Experiments on the WHU and Inria datasets reveal that HFER-SAM achieves an Intersection over Union of 91.53% and 82.06%, respectively. Our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in both accuracy and boundary fidelity, providing a robust avenue for high-precision building mapping.

title: Advancing Mangrove Forest Mapping Using Super-Resolution and Semantic Segmentation of Multi-Date Multi-Sensor Satellite Imagery: Applications in East and West Africa
summary: Remote sensing is essential for mapping mangrove forest ecosystems, yet accuracy and spatial resolution remain limited, particularly in Africa, where mangroves are fragmented, reference data and cloud-free images are scarce. The state-of-the-art of mangrove forest mapping relies on native-resolution imagery using machine learning. This study evaluates deep learning methods using aggregated multi-date satellite imagery to improve mangrove mapping and national-scale area estimation. Super-resolution and semantic segmentation techniques were applied to Sentinel-2 (S2) and Sentinel-1 (S1) images, with training data derived from field observations and high-resolution drone and satellite imagery. Coastal regions of Tanzania and Ghana were used as representative study areas for eastern and western Africa, respectively. Results show strong classification performance, with S2 imagery alone achieving an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 85.8%. Adding S1 provided modest gains (IoU 86.3%), while super-resolution significantly improved the accuracy (IoU 88.5%). The combined super-resolved S2 and S1 dataset yielded the highest performance (IoU 89.2%). Wall-to-wall mapping and statistically rigorous validation and area estimation produced accurate results with quantified uncertainty. Tanzania showed high consistency (F1 = 96%; 1207 km2, 95% CI [1151.7, 1263]), while Ghana exhibited slightly higher uncertainty (F1 = 92%; 92.6 km2, 95% CI [87.5, 97.7]). Integrating deep learning with multi-date, multi-sensor fusion and super-resolution enables accurate mangrove mapping and area estimation for improved coastal management and restoration.

title: Evaluation of the Landsat 8 Provisional Aquatic Reflectance Product for Inland Water Quality Monitoring
summary: The USGS Landsat 8 Provisional Aquatic Reflectance (PAR) product offers a standardized basis for inland water monitoring, but its reliability is constrained by spectral uncertainty and valid-data availability. This study evaluated PAR using GLORIA in situ observations, Lake Lanier field measurements, and cross-sensor comparisons, with ACOLITE and OC-SMART as alternative atmospheric correction methods. In the full GLORIA comparison, PAR showed median absolute percentage differences (MAPDs) of 115.9% and 75.2% at 443 and 483 nm, respectively, compared with 40.0% at 561 nm and 66.5% at 655 nm. Moreover, 310 of 579 PAR matchups contained negative reflectance in at least one band, substantially limiting usable observations. Water quality retrievals evaluated using common matchups yielded PAR MAPD values of 71.6% for chlorophyll-a, 71.0% for total suspended solids, and 117.7% for colored dissolved organic matter absorption, indicating substantial retrieval uncertainty even after sample availability was controlled. Over Lake Lanier, narrow water branches exhibited substantial PAR data loss and less reliable retrievals, highlighting limitations associated with shoreline proximity and mixed pixels. Differences in valid-data coverage also constrained direct comparisons among methods at this site. Cross-sensor comparisons over Lake Victoria and Lake Michigan, nevertheless, showed that PAR captured broad spatial patterns, while time-series comparisons suggested potential for resolving seasonal variability, particularly in chlorophyll-a. Overall, PAR may support monitoring of larger inland waters when sufficient valid observations are available. Applications in small or narrow waters, and retrievals sensitive to blue-band errors, require particular caution. Broader operational and long-term use requires further validation across sites and years.

title: SIF-Constrained Optimization of SCOPE Vegetation Parameters for Gross Primary Productivity Estimation
summary: Solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) provides a new pathway for the accurate estimation of gross primary productivity (GPP) by directly probing vegetation photosynthetic functioning, but mechanistic estimation is still constrained by the difficulty of obtaining the seasonal dynamics of key physiological parameters. Using maize, a representative C4 crop, as an experimental case, this study integrated long-term tower-based SIF observations with the SCOPE model to propose a cross-variable constraint strategy, in which key vegetation parameters were optimized against in situ SIF observations and independently validated against eddy covariance-derived GPP. Specifically, key sensitive parameters were first identified via Sobol global sensitivity analysis. A double-baseline asymmetric Gaussian phenology model was then constructed to characterize the seasonal dynamics of Vcmax, while Cab was derived from Vcmax using a smoothed piecewise-linear empirical relationship. A two-stage Bayesian optimization scheme was applied to optimize the parameters, which were subsequently used to run the SCOPE model and reconstruct continuous SIF and GPP time series. The results showed that the estimated daily SIF and GPP agreed well with ground observations, yielding R2 values of 0.86 and 0.74, respectively. Furthermore, the upscaled results correlated strongly with satellite products (MODIS: R = 0.94, R2 = −2.69; PML: R = 0.95, R2 = 0.81). This study demonstrates the feasibility of using SIF observations to constrain SCOPE vegetation parameters for improved GPP estimation, providing a parameterization basis and methodological support for mechanistic remote sensing monitoring of vegetation productivity.

title: Hyperspectral Retrieval of Winter Wheat Leaf Area Index and Canopy Chlorophyll Content: Evaluating Simulation Design and Measured-Data Adaptation
summary: How retrieval performance varies with simulation settings, neural architecture, and measured-data adaptation remains unclear for hyperspectral crop trait retrieval. Here, we evaluated winter wheat leaf area index (LAI) and canopy chlorophyll content (CCC) retrieval using two simulated datasets and four dual-branch neural architectures. Models were pretrained on two PROSAIL-D datasets with default and previously optimized leaf-angle settings and then adapted separately to ground and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) observations. Evaluation used five repetitions with physical-plot grouping, with approximately 30% of plot groups allocated to measured-data adaptation. Simulation-trained random forest (RF) and partial least squares regression served as baselines without measured-data adaptation. Adaptation reduced mean test root mean square error (RMSE) in all 32 neural model–dataset–target–platform combinations relative to direct simulation-based prediction. Dataset II, which used the previously optimized leaf-angle setting, reduced mean RMSE in 13 of 16 neural configurations before adaptation and 11 of 16 afterwards. No neural architecture was uniformly best. RF achieved the highest mean R2 in seven of eight simulation-only tasks and outperformed the adapted Dataset II CNN–Transformer on both UAV targets. Despite adaptation gains, all adapted neural configurations retained negative mean R2 for UAV CCC. These findings support measured-data adaptation within the tested protocol, while showing that the effects of simulation design and architecture are task dependent and that relative improvements do not necessarily imply adequate absolute predictive accuracy.

title: Reconstructing Missing Spectral Bands for Seamless Continuity Between GOCI and GOCI-II
summary: Establishing data continuity across satellite missions is essential for multi-decadal ocean color time-series. This study presents an integration framework to achieve radiometric harmonization and spectral continuity between the First and Second Geostationary Ocean Color Imagers (GOCI and GOCI-II) over the East China Sea. Using collocated observations during their mission overlap period, a two-step transformation scheme was established. First, systematic calibration offsets across six overlapping bands (412–680 nm) were eliminated by harmonizing GOCI to the GOCI-II via ordinary least-squares regression, bringing mean bias values near zeros (R2 > 0.95 and relative RMSD ≈ 12–13% in mid-visible bands). Second, GOCI remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) was expanded to reconstruct three GOCI-II-specific missing spectral bands (510, 620, and 709 nm) using two independent approaches: the physics-based Quasi-Analytical Algorithm (QAA) and Trust Region Reflective (TRR) optimization. Comparative validation demonstrated that the TRR model consistently outperformed QAA across dynamic coastal gradients. TRR achieved high spectral fidelity while suppressing coastal inversion errors. Furthermore, regional spectral curves verified that the harmonized and TRR-derived GOCI Rrs closely converged with GOCI-II Rrs across moderately turbid, highly turbid, and clear offshore waters. This framework verifies the feasibility of constructing a seamless geostationary ocean color database spanning GOCI and GOCI-II, establishing a solid foundation for long-term marine monitoring and future missions like GOCI-III.

title: OBB-PBD: Extending Parallel Box Decoding to Oriented Bounding Boxes for Referring Expression Grounding in Aerial Imagery
summary: Referring expression grounding in overhead imagery requires oriented bounding boxes rather than horizontal ones, since aerial objects appear at arbitrary orientations. Most grounding models emit box coordinates sequentially; Parallel Box Decoding (PBD) instead predicts all geometry slots in one forward pass, but only for four-coordinate horizontal boxes. We extend this block-aligned interface to a six-slot oriented representation using a double-angle parameterization. Rather than assuming correctness from a decreasing loss curve, we verify the extension with image/prompt-shuffle controls and visibility/leakage probes, which show that the corrected model depends on both the image and the prompt rather than on prompt statistics alone. On the aerial vehicle visual grounding (AVVG) benchmark, whose targets are genuinely oriented, the extended model improves rotated intersection over union (rotIoU) from 0.1253 for the zero-shot baseline to 0.303±0.012 (mean ± standard deviation over three training seeds) across the complete 6139-record test split spanning all 120 images. Learning oriented boxes rather than their axis-aligned envelopes adds 0.055±0.008 rotIoU beyond a matched control (per-seed 95% confidence intervals all excluding zero), whereas block expansion alone yields no rotIoU gain distinguishable from zero.

title: Three-Dimensional Multiscale Variational Analysis of Near-Space Temperature Using an MSIS Empirical Background and TIMED/SABER Profiles
summary: The near-space region is of strategic importance for aerospace activities. However, accurate temperature analyses remain challenging due to sparse observations and multiscale spatial structure. In this study, a multiscale variational analysis (MSVA) configuration is applied and evaluated for near-space temperature analyses using the Mass Spectrometer and Incoherent Scatter (MSIS) empirical model as the background field and TIMED/SABER temperature observations as observational constraints. The multiscale strategy is implemented via a prescribed sum of three-dimensional Gaussian background error covariance components with scale-dependent horizontal length scales and a common vertical coupling structure. A set of observing system simulation experiments (OSSEs) and experiments using real observations are conducted to assess MSVA in comparison with a single-scale variational analysis (SSVA). Results from the multistage OSSEs show that the multiscale covariance design improves the recovery of observation-supported structures. In the three-dimensional OSSE, MSVA reduces the global RMSE from 3.93 K for 1200 km SSVA to 3.78 K, and reduces the RMSE over withheld profiles from 3.56 K to 3.16 K. Using real SABER temperature observations, both three-dimensional analyses reduce MSIS–SABER observational space departures; the mean all-profile RMSE decreases from 11.43 K for MSIS to 5.97 K for 3D SSVA and 5.35 K for 3D MSVA. Comparison with unassimilated Aura/MLS observations gives corresponding RMSEs of 8.74, 7.60, and 7.39 K, providing an independent external evaluation of the analyses using real observations. These results demonstrate that representing multiple horizontal scales improves near-space temperature analysis relative to a single-scale formulation, as evidenced by controlled OSSEs and independent MLS evaluation.

title: Connectivity-Preserving Control-Network Thinning for Planetary Photogrammetry Using Image-Pair Convex Hulls and Grid Sampling
summary: The dense control networks constructed for regional and global image blocks often contain a substantial number of redundant tie points that increase the computational burden of bundle adjustment (BA). Reducing this redundancy without weakening the geometric support of image pairs is essential for subsequent photogrammetric processing. Existing image-centered network-thinning methods reduce point counts but do not explicitly preserve direct links between individual image pairs. This paper presents an efficient control-network thinning method for planetary photogrammetry based on image-pair convex-hull computation and grid-based interval sampling. The proposed method first organizes the input control network into an image-pair measure map. It then separates each pair’s measures into hull and interior classes using Andrew’s monotone-chain algorithm and samples the two classes at different intervals. When a tie point is selected for an image pair, its measures in both images are retained together. An optional rule can also retain measures of the same surface feature in other overlapping images to help maintain connections across the image block. The method is designed to thin an existing control network after upstream quality filtering. It does not re-evaluate tie-point quality or add new control points. We implemented the method as the cnetoptimize application within the Integrated Software for Imagers and Spectrometers (ISIS), a widely used open-source planetary photogrammetric software system developed by the United States Geological Survey (USGS). Experiments used a large-scale Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) Narrow Angle Camera (NAC) network and a medium-scale Mars Express (MEX) High Resolution Stereo Camera (HRSC) network. At comparable compression ratios, cnetoptimize retained strict non-degenerate support for more image pairs than the image-centered ISIS cnetthinner. Across the tested datasets and settings, cnetoptimize preserved the direct connections of all originally non-degenerate image pairs at compression ratios up to 8.4×. In a downstream test on one weak HRSC pair, bundle adjustment with the thinned cnetoptimize network yielded subpixel image residuals and a local 25 m digital orthophoto map (DOM) seam root mean square (RMS) of 36.0 m. The method provides an ISIS-compatible approach to control-network thinning for planetary mapping.

title: Assessment of Cropland Abandonment and Vegetation Recovery on the Chinese Loess Plateau
summary: Cropland abandonment alters agricultural land use and may enable improvements in vegetation cover. On the Chinese Loess Plateau, the extent and spatial variation of these changes remain critical questions for land management. This study used annual land-cover trajectories to identify persistent cropland withdrawal from 2000 to 2020 and Landsat-derived fractional vegetation cover (FVC) to assess vegetation change. The total first-abandonment area was 80,700.64 km2, and the annual area of first abandonment peaked in 2004 at 7176.16 km2 and subsequently declined amid interannual fluctuations, with abandoned cropland concentrated on gentle slopes. Across five representative years, the mean FVC of land classified as abandoned each year rose from 0.273 in 2000 to 0.381 in 2020. These values reflect changes in pixel populations rather than the trajectory of a fixed set of fields. Among pixels mapped as abandoned in 2020, 86.07% showed increasing FVC over the entire study period, including 60.12% with significant increases. Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) analysis with Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) identified precipitation as the strongest predictor of spatial variation in the FVC change rate, accounting for 39.6% of the model’s relative importance. SHAP dependence patterns showed model-based transition points at approximately 395 mm of precipitation and 10 °C of temperature. These findings characterize vegetation-cover change associated with abandoned land and its environmental variation, whereas the full-period trends cannot isolate vegetation change caused by abandonment.

title: Cross-Resolution Fusion of AlphaEarth Foundations Embeddings and GF-1 Imagery via Semantic Anchor-Graph Enhancement for Litchi Orchard Extraction
summary: Litchi is an important cash crop in China. Accurate litchi orchard extraction is crucial for agricultural management and economic development. However, litchi orchards are spectrally very similar to evergreen broad-leaved forests and are poorly resolved in medium- and low-resolution satellite imagery, so large-scale extraction remains challenging. A cross-resolution fusion network via semantic anchor-graph enhancement (SAGE-Net) is therefore proposed, using a dual-branch encoder–decoder to aggregate complementary features of AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) embeddings and GF-1 imagery. To enable semantic interaction across resolutions, the SAGE module is designed to gather the AEF embeddings into a few semantic anchors, reason over the anchor graph, and scatter them back under GF-1 guidance, so that semantic content and spatial extent are supplied by the source better suited to each. To refine the coarse prediction to full resolution without discarding what is already reliable, the reliability-adaptive correction (RAC) head is designed to gate a detail-guided correction by the confidence and local consistency of that prediction, concentrating refinement where it is uncertain. In Shenzhen, SAGE-Net attains the highest IoU (0.5660) and F1-score (0.7229) among eight comparison methods, with a Precision of 0.7162 and a Recall of 0.7297. Under stricter protocols that separate the training and the evaluation patches by a 256 m buffer or by whole spatial blocks, the IoU falls to 0.5224 and 0.5000 and SAGE-Net remains the most accurate of the networks retested, by a smaller margin. The results demonstrate the value of role-aware enhancement and reliability-adaptive correction for fine-grained orchard mapping, and confirm AEF embeddings as an effective supplementary data source for large-scale mapping.

title: Ground-Deconvolved GEDI Waveforms Reveal Ladder Fuel Structure in Open Dry Dipterocarp Forest: A Ground-to-Space Sensor Comparison
summary: Dry dipterocarp forest (DDF) in mainland Southeast Asia burns frequently in surface fires, yet the vertical fuel strata observable from airborne and spaceborne sensors remain uncertain. We compared handheld SLAM LiDAR, UAV LiDAR, GEDI, ICESat-2, PlanetScope, and Sentinel-1/2 at Sakaerat, Thailand, using spatial block-bootstrap validation. SLAM and UAV LiDAR converged on the 1–2 m and 2–5 m strata (r = 0.53 for both, n = 212) but not below 0.5 m, identifying the 2–5 m ladder fuel fraction as the strongest cross-platform target. Optical models explained at most 32% of understory and 37% of ladder fuel variance, with no benefit from finer pixels or Sentinel-1. GEDI relative-height metrics failed below 2 m because the ground return was broad (mean FWHM 4.2 m) and widened with slope. Subtracting a fitted ground Gaussian recovered a reproducible 1–5 m waveform signal correlated with UAV ladder fuel in both 2025 (ρ = 0.47) and 2026 (ρ = 0.42), robust across detection thresholds and fitting windows. Only 22% of regional GEDI footprints supported two-mode canopy-base detection, while ICESat-2 showed the same height-ordered sensitivity. In this open DDF stand, remote sensing was therefore best suited to ladder fuel and vertical continuity; near-surface fuel requires ground-based observation.

title: SDFNet: Semantic Driven Frequency-Domain Infrared and Visible Image Fusion Network
summary: Infrared and visible image fusion aims to integrate complementary thermal target information and visible structural details for multimodal perception and remote sensing applications. However, existing deep learning methods often underutilize semantic information during fusion and mainly perform cross-modal interaction in the spatial domain, limiting the exploitation of complementary representations. To address these issues, we propose SDFNet, a semantic driven frequency-domain infrared and visible image fusion network based on an encoder–decoder architecture. Guided by semantic priors extracted from a pre-trained segmentation model, SDFNet introduces a frequency-domain feature aggregation module to enhance cross-modal feature interaction and semantic information preservation. Extensive experiments on the MSRS dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. On the 361-pair MSRS test set, SDFNet ranks among the top two on five of the six evaluated fusion metrics, achieving EN, AG, SF, SCD, and Qabf scores of 6.73, 3.78, 11.59, 1.74, and 0.69, respectively, while obtaining a competitive VIF score of 1.02. In the downstream semantic utility evaluation, SDFNet achieves the highest mIoU of 78.76 among the compared methods, further demonstrating its ability to preserve task-relevant semantic information.

title: Process-Inspired Latent Dynamics for Direct Multi-Step Regional Sea Surface Temperature Forecasting
summary: Sea surface temperature (SST) forecasts support marine environmental monitoring, hazard assessment, and operational ocean services. Regional multi-step prediction remains difficult because SST-only models must represent transport, spatial spreading, and local nonlinear variation from historical fields while avoiding the recursive use of predicted states. We propose ADR-Net, a direct multi-step forecasting model that combines a flexible data-driven stream with a process-inspired advection–diffusion–reaction (ADR) stream in a shared latent bottleneck. The ADR stream organizes latent SST evolution through three operators that represent transport-like displacement, spatial spreading, and local nonlinear variation. A temporal projection module (TPM) then projects the fused latent representation and multi-scale encoder features directly to all forecast leads. We evaluated ADR-Net against eight learned baselines and two non-learned references using daily OISST v2.1 data from the East China Sea (ECS), South China Sea (SCS), Niño 1+2, and Niño 3.4 regions. Separate models were trained with output lengths L∈{1,7,13}. ADR-Net achieved the lowest MSE, MAE, and RMSE in all 12 region–output length settings across four regions and three output lengths. In the ECS, it reduced the MSE by 1.46%, 8.07%, and 5.70% relative to the best MSE baseline for L=1, L=7, and L=13, respectively. For the ECS L=13 task, ADR-Net maintained the lowest MAE and highest SSIM at every lead day and extended the mean effective forecast horizon from 3.91 to 4.49 days under grid cell thresholds of RMSE ≤ 0.7 °C and R2≥0.95. Component ablations on the ECS seven-day task showed that removing the TPM or the process-inspired ADR stream increased the mean MSE by 4.55% and 3.86%, respectively, while removing both increased it by 8.32%. ADR-Net used 7.09 million parameters and 13.07 GFLOPs per ECS seven-day forecast sample. Across four storm-associated episodes, ADR-Net achieved the lowest event-mean cooling footprint MAE at every forecast lead from day 1 to day 13. Together, these results support the combination of process-inspired latent modeling and direct temporal projection for accurate, spatially coherent regional SST forecasting.

title: ENSO-Flavor Differences in Indonesian Marine Heatwaves: Satellite SST, Physical Covariates, and Coral Habitat Suitability
summary: Marine heatwaves (MHWs) in the Indonesian Seas develop within a long-term rise in sea surface temperature and strong interannual climate variability. We analyze daily NOAA Optimum Interpolation Sea Surface Temperature version 2.1 for 1982–2022 and compare five Eastern-Pacific (EP) with five Central-Pacific (CP) El Niño events. MHWs are detected against a fixed 1982–2011 baseline, and each event is represented by the common 1 July–30 June window spanning its developing and decaying phases. EP-minus-CP differences are 14.25 area-weighted MHW days and 22.34 °C·days of cumulative intensity. Their event-bootstrap intervals span zero, the exact permutation tests are nonsignificant, and no grid cell passes false-discovery-rate control for either metric. Annual MHW days increase by an area-weighted 11.37 days per decade; 90.5% of the domain passes false-discovery-rate control, and the temporal-block field test yields p=0.001. The increase remains widespread after linear Niño-3.4 and dipole-mode-index adjustment. Direct physical diagnostics, spatial-block habitat validation, and official Fisheries Management Area (FMA) summaries are used to assess the strength and limitations of the proposed process and management interpretations. The physical-diagnostic intervals include zero, and the MaxEnt output represents modeled environmental suitability. The results establish a spatially extensive long-term increase in MHW exposure and quantify the uncertainty in the event-scale physical and ecological pathways.

title: Moderate Resolution Satellites Monitor Vegetation Phenology Accurately in African Savannas: A Comparison with Ground Data from Phenocams
summary: Reliable monitoring of leaf phenology across environmental gradients is essential for understanding ecosystem functioning and climate responses, yet existing approaches in African savannas are constrained by either sparse ground-based observations or the limited resolution of satellite products. We evaluated the ability of MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer), VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite), and Sentinel-2-derived vegetation indices (Normalised-Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), Enhanced Vegetation Index (EVI), and Green Chromatic Coordinate (GCC)) to track phenocam-derived phenology across 10 plots along a water-availability gradient in Africa. Satellite vegetation index time series were smoothed using generalized additive models and compared with phenocam-derived GCC, including estimates of transition dates. All satellite datasets estimated longer growing seasons than phenocams, associated with earlier start-of-season (SOS) and later end-of-season (EOS) estimates. MODIS NDVI and VIIRS NDVI most accurately estimated transition dates (SOS root-mean-squared error (RMSE), a standard measure of model accuracy, of 10 and 11 days, respectively; EOS RMSE of 27 days in both datasets). MODIS GCC and VIIRS EVI followed with high estimated transition date accuracy (SOS RMSE of 11 days; EOS RMSE of 32 days, in both datasets). VIIRS EVI and Sentinel-2 (S2) GCC most accurately tracked phenocam temporal fluctuations (r = 0.83 ± 0.08 and 0.83 ± 0.10, respectively), while MODIS GCC and MODIS NDVI also showed high correlations (r = 0.78 ± 0.12 and 0.78 ± 0.15). These MODIS products tracked intraseasonal fluctuations more closely than the VIIRS and S2 datasets. We consider MODIS NDVI the most accurate dataset overall, given its accuracy in estimating SOS and EOS, visible tracking of intraseasonal fluctuations, and high temporal correlation with phenocam phenology. These results support using MODIS and VIIRS for large-scale phenology monitoring and upscaling phenocam observations in African savannas.

title: TLS and UAV Photogrammetry for As-Built Mapping of Wastewater Treatment Infrastructure: A Comparative Assessment and Retrospective Source Selection Approach
summary: Terrestrial laser scanning (TLS) and unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) photogrammetry provide complementary observations for infrastructure documentation, but their suitability depends on the required map features. This study compares TLS- and UAV-derived as-built products for a wastewater treatment plant with a conventional survey reference and illustrates a preliminary, retrospective, feature-level data source selection approach. Positional agreement was assessed at 30 independent check points selected purposively from details identifiable in all three products. RMSE3D was 7.51 cm for TLS and 7.66 cm for UAV; these values characterize the common observable sample rather than the accuracy of the complete infrastructure. TLS and UAV mapped 128 and 102 of 135 reference objects, corresponding to object detection completeness rates of 94.8% and 75.6%, respectively. UAV required less recorded acquisition effort, while TLS recovered more reference objects using the tested configuration. A transparent score combines planimetric accuracy and object detection completeness where both are available, with source eligibility assessed separately. The application illustrates source comparison using existing products; it does not establish improved map quality or lower production cost. A completed selected source map and a merge-all alternative were not independently evaluated.

title: A UAV-Assisted FP-xLSTM Framework for Spatio-Temporal Prediction of Multi-Depth Urban River Water Quality
summary: Effective water quality monitoring is essential for protecting aquatic environments and supporting sustainable management of urban rivers. Accurate prediction and visualization of water quality parameters (WQPs) distributions across spatial, temporal, and vertical dimensions remained challenging for unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)-based remote sensing approaches, which often neglected depth-wise variability and required extensive water sampling to maintain stable prediction performance for multiple WQPs. To address these limitations, this study proposed a feature propagation-based extended long short-term memory framework (FP-xLSTM) for unified prediction and visualization of multi-depth WQPs, including total phosphorus (TP), total nitrogen (TN), chlorophyll-a (Chl-a), chemical oxygen demand (COD), biochemical oxygen demand (BOD), and total suspended solids (TSS). By integrating spectral characteristics with spatio-temporal dependencies through feature propagation across consecutive temporal observations, FP-xLSTM effectively captured short-term fluctuations and learned vertical distribution patterns of heterogeneous WQPs from multi-source data while reducing sampling requirements. A field study with an eight-month interval between the first and last sampling campaigns was conducted to evaluate the proposed framework under cross-region experimental settings and against state-of-the-art baseline models. Results demonstrated that FP-xLSTM consistently outperformed competing methods, achieving average coefficients of determination (R2) ranging from 0.66 to 0.95 and mean absolute percentage errors (MAPE) between 9.33% and 19.06%. Furthermore, the framework has potential for deployment in practical environmental monitoring applications to support local environmental authorities in tracking river water quality dynamics and optimizing management strategies. Overall, the proposed method provided an effective and scalable intelligent framework for UAV-assisted urban water quality assessment and multi-depth environmental visualization.

title: SDFNet: Snow Depth Retrieval Based on a Multi-Scale Feature Fusion Network for the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau
summary: High-resolution snow depth (SD) information supports hydrological and cryospheric studies in complex mountain regions. Coarse SD products limit representation of terrain-related snow variability in these environments. This study proposes SDFNet, a Snow Depth Fusion Network combining Sentinel-1 SAR, Landsat optical data, digital elevation model (DEM) variables, and fractional snow cover (FSC). Multi-scale feature extraction, channel enhancement, and feature aggregation modules represent relationships among these inputs. Observations from 95 meteorological stations across the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau supplied supervision and reference measurements for evaluation. Station SD was the regression target rather than a prediction input. In the station-based comparison, SDFNet achieved an RMSE of 5.246 cm and an R2 of 0.702. It had the lowest RMSE and highest R2 among the compared models. However, SD above 40 cm produced an RMSE of 21.927 cm and a bias of −16.061 cm, indicating substantial deep-snow underestimation. Sparse station coverage limits inference beyond the sampled environments, and independent spatial validation remains necessary.

title: Wave as Disturbance and Signal in a Physics-Informed Framework for Shallow Water Bathymetry
summary: Satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) commonly treats the sea surface as a source of radiometric disturbance, although the same surface wave field can also contain water depth information through gravity wave propagation. This article presents a Wave-Aware Physics-Informed Neural Network (WA-PINN) that represents these two roles within a unified shallow water bathymetry framework. The optical geometry stream combines Sentinel-2 multispectral observations with seafloor geometry. The disturbance stream converts European Centre for Medium Range Weather Forecasts Reanalysis Version 5 (ERA5) wind forcing into Mean Square Slope (MSS) through the Cox–Munk relationship and introduces a roughness-dependent sunglint contribution into the optical physics constraint. The signal stream retrieves local wavelength, propagation direction, and wave celerity from Sentinel-2 surface texture and constrains predicted depth with the finite depth gravity wave dispersion relation. A Wave Validity Factor (WVF) controls the influence of the dispersion constraint according to the coherence and physical plausibility of the retrieved wave field. The three streams are fused in a shared depth predictor constrained by supervised depth loss, optical physics loss, and wave dispersion physics loss. The framework is demonstrated over Culebra, St. Thomas, and St. John in the northeastern Caribbean Sea. The complete Dual Role model reaches an overall Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 1.21 m, a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) 0.77 m, and an R2 of 0.96. Relative to the Slope Aware configuration, the Disturbance and Signal models reduce RMSE by 15.7% and 12.8%, while the complete model reduces RMSE by 29.7%. The disturbance contribution increases under stronger wind forcing, whereas the signal contribution increases with WVF. Depth-dependent RMSE increases from 0.82 m at 0 to 5 m to 1.58 m at 20 to 30 m. These results illustrate the intended complementarity between correcting wave-induced optical contamination and exploiting wave propagation as an additional depth constraint.

title: Classification and Remote Sensing Characterization of Large Catastrophic Landslides in the Southeastern Tibetan Plateau, China
summary: Large catastrophic landslides in the southeastern Tibetan Plateau are characterized by huge volumes and complex chains that frequently cause river damming and casualties. Based on field surveys, multi-temporal satellite imagery, Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV), Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) deformation measurements, and meteorological and seismic records, this study classifies these landslides into three types by their initiation and disaster-chain processes: (1) rock–ice avalanche → debris flow → landslide dam; (2) debris flow → landslide dam; (3) rock avalanche → landslide dam. Representative cases illustrate the material sources, initiation settings, and downstream impacts of each type. The occurrence of such landslides is influenced by the interplay of four groups of factors: fractured rock masses and abundant loose deposits provide the material basis; high mountains and narrow river valleys provide the spatial framework for landslide evolution and promote river blockage; pronounced climatic changes provide the background conditions and may affect slope stability in glaciated areas through glacier retreat; and frequent strong earthquakes can both instantaneously trigger failure and cause cumulative damage that predisposes slopes to subsequent failures. Ongoing climate warming and repeated seismic activity are expected to increase landslide susceptibility, highlighting the urgency of multi-hazard early warning and proactive mitigation. This study supports early warning prioritization and risk governance in high-mountain valleys across the Tibetan Plateau.

title: Long-Term Mangrove Dynamics and Environmental Associations in the Sundarbans, Bangladesh: Integrating Remote Sensing, Machine Learning, and Explainable AI
summary: Mangrove ecosystems are increasingly threatened by anthropogenic disturbances and climate change, despite providing ecological services, including biodiversity conservation, coastal protection, and blue carbon storage. Long-term evaluations of mangrove dynamics and associated environmental conditions remain limited, particularly in the Sundarbans, the largest mangrove forest in the world. This study examined the spatiotemporal dynamics of the Sundarbans mangrove ecosystem, Bangladesh, using multi-temporal Landsat imagery (1990–2025), Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP). Model performance was evaluated using the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) dataset and spatially blocked holdout validation. Classification accuracy was high (94.56–100%) under internal and spatially blocked validation (93.5–99.8%), whereas comparison with GMW yielded lower accuracies (66.4–95.7%). Change detection showed that mangrove area expanded from 2096.66 km2 in 1990 to 3875.95 km2 in 2025, a net gain of almost 1779.29 km2, with substantial inter-period variability and a pronounced mapped decline between 2000 and 2005. SHAP analysis indicated that the relative contributions of model predictors changed over time, with NDVI contributing more strongly to model predictions in recent years than NDWI and NDMI. Mangrove gain, loss, and net change were statistically associated with cyclone exposure and elevation, while precipitation and river discharge showed less consistent relationships. This study highlights a practical method for monitoring spectral dynamics in vulnerable coastal ecosystems and supports mangrove conservation.

title: Adaptive LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS SLAM Framework for Georeferenced Mapping in Challenging Urban Environments
summary: Maintaining accurate, georeferenced dense maps requires reliable global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) observations to constrain global drift. Degraded observations must be prevented from distorting trajectories and local maps as reception transitions from open sky to urban obstruction and complete signal denial indoors. This study develops and evaluates Dense LiDAR–Inertial–GNSS simultaneous localization and mapping (DLIG-SLAM) to adapt GNSS integration and local mapping as reception conditions change. Built on Dense Multi-Scan Adjustment, the framework estimates the local trajectory and dense map separately from the transformation that connects them to a global coordinate frame. GNSS observations are assessed separately for updating this transformation and correcting the estimator. An online switcher selects among integration strategies according to measurement reliability, estimator readiness, and trajectory consistency. Outdoor–indoor state changes reconfigure local mapping, while voxel size adapts to the observed scan point population. Evaluation was performed on four KITTI driving sequences and an urban canyon outdoor–indoor mission in Toronto, recorded with standalone single-point positioning GNSS. GNSS coupling through an inertial navigation estimate achieved the lowest three-dimensional trajectory root mean square error on three of the four KITTI sequences. Online switching did not consistently outperform fixed integration strategies in the KITTI trajectory evaluation. In the Toronto dataset, inertial navigation-mediated coupling achieved the lowest horizontal georeferencing root mean square error of 1.29 m, while full-navigation factor graph smoothing achieved the lowest three-dimensional georeferencing root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.71 m. Online switching achieved the lowest cloud-to-cloud root mean square distance of 6.1 cm against a terrestrial laser scanning reference within the evaluated facade and ground floor region. Controlled experiments also evaluated the effect of separate GNSS admission paths and global transformation policies. The results support adapting GNSS integration to changing reception conditions and mapping objectives, as stronger coupling did not uniformly improve trajectory accuracy, global placement, and local geometric agreement.

title: High-Resolution Multiscale Seismic Fracture Prediction via Basis Pursuit Frequency Extension-Enhanced Multi-Attribute Fusion
summary: Fractures are important storage spaces and flow pathways in tight reservoirs, but small-scale fractures with weak seismic responses are difficult to characterize with band-limited post-stack seismic data. This study proposes a high-resolution multiscale seismic method for predicting fracture distribution based on basis pursuit frequency extension (BPFE)-enhanced multi-attribute fusion. BPFE represents each trace sparsely on a wedge dictionary built from a zero-phase Morlet wavelet, which is derived from the average dominant frequency of the data. It then re-synthesizes the basis pursuit denoising solution with a time-compressed wavelet, thereby extending the effective bandwidth without estimating the seismic wavelet. Dip-steered third-generation coherence and ant-tracking attributes are subsequently normalized and fused with explicit weights according to their attribute-sensitive scales, and objective rules are provided for selecting the BPFE parameters. Synthetic tests with known reflectivity show that BPFE reproduces the ideal high-resolution section with correlation coefficients of 0.978 (noise-free) and 0.882 (signal-to-noise ratio of 10 dB). BPFE increases the dominant frequency from 30.8 to 49.3 Hz and reduces the tuning thickness from 16 to 11 ms without systematic phase rotation. At 10 dB, it also raises the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve for detecting weak bed-confined discontinuities from 0.580 to 0.687, outperforming spectral whitening, spiking deconvolution, inverse-Q filtering and sparse-spike inversion in this respect. Applied to the tight sandstone reservoir in the northeastern Sichuan Basin, the workflow delineates main faults, fault-associated fracture zones and small-scale discontinuities more completely than coherence, ant tracking or their fusion without BPFE, which is consistent with the actual geological understanding. The workflow offers a wavelet-estimation-free approach for characterizing weak-response small-scale fractures, although its generalization requires further field validation.

title: A Lightweight Coastal Litter Segmentation Network with Feature Gating and Multiscale Context for UAV Imagery
summary: Litter stranded on beaches can severely degrade local ecosystems and diminish the tourism value of coastal areas. The integration of deep learning into unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) provides an effective means for the automatic segmentation of coastal litter. However, large variations in litter scale and complex coastal backgrounds lead to relatively low detection accuracy. In addition, most existing detection models require substantial computational resources, which limits their deployment. To address these issues, we constructed a coastal litter segmentation dataset and developed a lightweight segmentation model, CoastalLitterNet. The dataset contains litter objects of different sizes, colors, and shapes, with various backgrounds. In CoastalLitterNet, a Lightweight Asymmetric U-shaped Backbone Network (L-Net) was designed to reduce model complexity, and Atrous Spatial Pyramid Pooling (ASPP) was introduced to segment litter objects at different scales. A CoastalLitterGate (CLG) was proposed to enhance litter-related features and improve adaptability to complex backgrounds. Comparative experiments showed that the mIoU, IoU1 and F1 of CoastalLitterNet reached 93.95%, 88.42% and 93.85%, respectively. The Params and FLOPs of the model are only 12.90 M and 189.30 G, respectively. The quantitative and qualitative results show that CoastalLitterNet effectively segments litter objects at varying scales and adapts well to complex coastal environments while maintaining a lightweight architecture.

title: Improving Open-Set Recognition in Long-Tailed Underwater Optical Monitoring via Frequency-Shrunk Prototypes and Group-Conditional Risk Calibration
summary: Camera-based underwater optical monitoring enables persistent and non-invasive observation of marine communities, but its automated interpretation is challenged by two coupled uncertainties: the natural long-tailed frequency distribution of observed organisms and the appearance of categories absent from model development. Rare known categories provide insufficient observations for reliably estimating class location and dispersion, whereas dominant categories may form broad acceptance regions that absorb previously unseen organisms. We propose Frequency-Shrunk Prototype and Risk Calibration (FSPRC), a known-only post hoc framework for long-tailed underwater optical monitoring built on an ImageNet-pretrained ConvNeXt-Tiny. FSPRC regularizes each empirical feature direction toward its corresponding classifier direction and shrinks its intraclass radius toward a frequency-group reference, with both corrections controlled by the number of training observations. Local prototype deviation and global energy evidence are then robustly normalized within the predicted head, middle, or tail group and combined without a trainable fusion module. Independent known-only calibration subsets determine group-conditional rejection thresholds, while held-out categories remain excluded from backbone adaptation, checkpoint selection, geometric estimation, score normalization, and threshold fitting. On the predefined fold-0 leakage-controlled protocols for AQUA20 and the track-disjoint Fish4Knowledge-23 dataset, FSPRC achieves open-set accuracies of 83.31% and 98.19%, open-set classification rate (OSCR) values of 85.96% and 98.96%, and unknown category macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values of 92.62% and 99.55%, respectively. Across exhaustive class-held-out partitions, open-set accuracy is 83.25±0.24% over four AQUA20 folds and 98.18±0.08% over five Fish4Knowledge-23 folds. These results demonstrate that frequency-dependent geometric stabilization and risk calibration can improve the recognition-stage balance between retaining data-scarce known organisms and referring unfamiliar observations for subsequent expert inspection.

title: Label-Free Quantitative Evaluation of Land Cover Segmentation Models for Remote Sensing Imagery: A Context-Aware Model Based on OpenStreetMap and a Digital Surface Model
summary: Segmentation performance is measured against pixel-wise ground truth (GT); without it, that measurement cannot be made. Remote sensing segmentation models are evaluated likewise, yet operational systems receive new unlabeled images, and the properties of those images shift with season, region, and sensor aging. A way to check performance outside the training dataset is needed. We propose quantifying segmentation output without labels, using public geospatial data: a random-forest context-aware model predicts class area composition from OpenStreetMap (OSM) and digital surface model (DSM) statistics. Quantile mapping transforms its output to match the distribution of measured compositions, yielding the expected distribution, and the Label-Free Composition Score (LFCS) is the similarity between that distribution and the composition of the segmentation output. The context-aware model is fitted only to geospatial features and GT compositions from the segmentation model’s training dataset, so the expected distribution is independent of the segmentation model’s structure, parameters, and outputs while depending on that dataset’s GT, class scheme, and composition distribution. The evaluation stage requires no GT labels. To test the method, we saved 430 segmentation model checkpoints from 75 training runs under six controlled training variations, so that the mean intersection over union (mIoU) of each, measured against GT on validation tiles held out of training, was known in advance. These GT mIoU values ranged from 0.04 to 0.69. The models were grouped by GT mIoU in steps of 0.1. Their mean LFCS rose with every step: from 0.474 to 0.937 on held-out images from the same dataset, and from 0.467 to 0.893 on 900 globally distributed unlabeled images. Existing measures that read only a model’s own output tracked GT mIoU less consistently. Rebuilding the entire method reproduced the same behavior on two public datasets with different class schemes, confirming the validity of the method under the conditions tested.

title: Fallen Tree Detection and Mapping from Airborne Laser Scanning Point Clouds Using Physics-Guided Supervoxel Learning
summary: Accurate fallen tree detection from airborne laser scanning (ALS) point clouds is important for forest structural assessment and disturbance monitoring. However, fallen trees remain difficult to extract from operational ALS data because near-ground stems are often fragmented by understory occlusion, uneven sampling, and geometric confusion with shrubs, terrain surfaces, and other low vegetation. This study proposes a physics-guided supervoxel framework for fallen tree detection from ALS point clouds. The framework represents ALS observations as spatially coherent supervoxels and describes each supervoxel using local geometric features, cylindrical morphology, and graph-based neighborhood context. Cylindrical descriptors encode the elongated stem structure of fallen trees, while graph-topological features represent spatial continuity among adjacent supervoxels. A stacking ensemble classifier is trained with SHAP-based feature selection, followed by graph-constrained spatial refinement to improve local label consistency. The framework was trained using 30 plots and evaluated on seven held-out forest plots from the Dutch Actueel Hoogtebestand Nederland 4 (AHN4) dataset, with point densities of 10–15 pts/m2. Using point-level reference labels, the stacking classifier achieved a mean fallen tree F1-score of 83.86% across the test plots, which increased to 85.39% after spatial refinement. Ablation results show that cylindrical descriptors provided the largest gain, improving the fallen tree F1 score by 11.77%. These results indicate that physics-guided supervoxel learning can produce interpretable fallen tree maps from operational ALS data and support subsequent analyses of near-ground forest structure and disturbance effects.

title: CAP-DBNet: A Class-Adaptive Prototype-Guided Dual-Branch Collaborative Network for Remote Sensing Image Semantic Segmentation
summary: High-resolution remote sensing image semantic segmentation faces challenges from large-scale variation, fine boundary preservation, and class imbalance. This paper proposes CAP-DBNet, a compact framework that combines a RepViT M2.3 backbone with a global–local collaborative decoder (GLCD), a class-adaptive hybrid loss (CAHL), and a class-adaptive prototype-guided calibration module (CAPC). CAP-DBNet integrates class-center global and window-local modeling through bidirectional feature exchange, mini-batch class-frequency-aware supervision, and prototype-based residual calibration. Rather than introducing an isolated new attention or prototype mechanism, this work focuses on the coordinated design of these components within an efficient segmentation framework. In five repeated experiments with different random seeds, CAP-DBNet achieves average mIoUs of 85.16%, 88.32%, and 55.75% on Vaihingen, Potsdam, and LoveDA, respectively, improving over the same-backbone LOGCAN++ baseline by 1.43, 1.24, and 1.44 percentage points. Compared with D2LS under our evaluation protocol, CAP-DBNet uses 3.55× fewer parameters and requires 8.35× fewer floating-point operations (FLOPs). These results demonstrate an accuracy-efficiency-oriented global–local and class-adaptive framework for remote sensing semantic segmentation across three public benchmarks.

title: Spectral Proxy Parameter Linking Remote Sensing Reflectance and Inherent Optical Properties in Case-2 Waters
summary: A spectral proxy parameter linking remote sensing reflectance (Rrs) and inherent optical properties (IOPs) was evaluated for six selected areas of the Baltic Sea. Measured IOPs from the individual optical datasets were used to calculate Morel’s unscaled proxy reflectance, whereas area and wavelength specific median IOPs were used as representative inputs to Monte Carlo radiative transfer simulations. Comparison of the individual proxy estimates with the corresponding area-specific Monte Carlo reference reflectance enabled determination of the spectral proxy parameter k. The results demonstrate a clear wavelength dependence and substantial area to area variability of this parameter. The purpose of the study is not to introduce a new fundamental IOPs–Rrs relationship, but to quantify how the effective scaling coefficient of a widely used proxy relationship varies spectrally and regionally in optically complex Case-2 waters. For each investigated Baltic Sea area, the spectral variability of k was approximated using a three-coefficient second-order polynomial. Area-specific parameterizations provide compact descriptions of the regional median k spectra, while a generalized formulation describes only the pooled central tendency. A radiometric evaluation was performed using 24 in situ OCP-100 spectra from the Gulf of Gdańsk (N = 96 wavelength-level pairs). Predicted and measured Rrs yielded r = 0.680, R2 = 0.462, a regression slope of 0.258, a mean bias of −0.00475 sr−1, an RMSE of 0.00590 sr−1, and a MAPE of 62.1%. Within-wavelength correlations were weak at 555 and 620 nm (r = 0.140 and 0.067, respectively). Thus, the regional parameterization preserves broad spectral ordering but underestimates absolute Rrs and does not establish strong station-level predictive skill. The results should be interpreted as a regional, configuration-dependent spectral scaling framework.

title: ChangeMoE: A Mixture-of-Experts-Based Mamba Network for Building Change Detection from High-Resolution Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Mamba has recently become a popular visual representation architecture for building change detection (BCD) in the remote sensing field. Although it effectively models global spatial dependencies, it still struggles to capture fine-grained local structures, thereby limiting its representation capability. To overcome this limitation, we propose ChangeMoE, a mixture-of-experts-based Mamba network for BCD from high-resolution remote sensing imagery. The main contributions and innovations are as follows: (1) A scan-specific mixture-of-experts (ScanMoE) module is proposed, which leverages a scan gating network to enhance global feature representations using eight selective scan mechanisms defined as scan-specific experts. We further quantify their contributions to improve the interpretability of global representation learning. (2) A global-and-local mixture-of-experts (GLMoE) module is proposed. We design the local and global expert networks to capture local details and global dependencies. A gating network is used to reveal their relative importance and adaptively fuse their complementary features. Experimental results on the LEVIR-CD and WHU-CD benchmarks validate the superiority of ChangeMoE over existing state-of-the-art networks. ChangeMoE achieves F1-scores of 92.55% and 94.11%, with IoU values of 86.13% and 88.88%, respectively. Compared with ChangeMamba as the baseline, the proposed ChangeMoE achieves improvements of 1.96% in F1-score and 3.33% in IoU on the LEVIR-CD dataset. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ChangeMoE and provide an interpretable expert-fusion paradigm for understanding feature representation learning in BCD.

title: QASHI: Quality-Aware Scale-Protected Hybrid Inference for Small-Object Detection in Optical and SAR Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Object detection in high-resolution remote sensing imagery faces a resolution–context trade-off: resizing weakens small objects, whereas cropping can truncate targets and remove context. We present QASHI, a detector-retraining-free hybrid inference framework combining a full-image view, four overlapping tiles, and at most three additional regions of interest (ROIs). Quality-Aware Density (QAD) prioritizes local re-inference by combining small-candidate density with weak responses, candidate competition, and full/tile prediction inconsistency. Graph-based ranking correction, bounded BoxVote refinement, and scale-protected routing integrate local predictions with full-image context. Experiments cover VisDrone2019-DET, DIOR, SeaDronesSee v2, and SRSDD-v1.0 with two RT-DETR detectors. On VisDrone-val with RT-DETRv4-S, QASHI improves AP by 2.84 points over the SAHI baseline while reducing mean latency by 14.40%. Relative to Full, it gains 5.74 AP points at 4.52 times the latency. Selector ablations and local parameter analyses characterize how region priority and fusion settings affect detection accuracy and computational cost. On SRSDD, display-domain image-quality sensitivity tests with RT-DETR-R50 yield higher mean perturbed AP (32.52 versus 31.41), with relative AP retention of 93.44% versus 93.98%. QASHI combines prediction-guided local processing and source-aware fusion to improve remote sensing detection through inference-time use of a fixed detector.

title: Machine Learning-Based Soil Moisture Inversion in Agro-Pastoral Areas Using Sentinel Data
summary: Soil moisture is a critical regulator in Earth’s energy cycle, exerting substantial influence on hydrological, ecological, and thermal processes. However, the spatio-temporal heterogeneity of soil moisture poses significant challenges for remote-sensing inversion, and conventional methods are constrained under complex surface conditions. In this study, Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 imagery were integrated with terrain data, and machine learning algorithms were employed to develop a soil moisture estimation model for the agro-pastoral transition zone. The primary objectives were to evaluate the accuracy of machine learning approaches for remote-sensing estimation of soil moisture under complex surface conditions, and to assess the suitability of different machine learning algorithms for this application. The results showed that ensemble methods, specifically boosting approaches, delivered low inversion errors and high R2 values, whereas linear models showed limited accuracy. The vertically polarized microwave backscattering coefficients emerged as the parameters most sensitive to soil moisture variations, with optical bands and topographic factors also making substantial contributions. The overall inversion yielded a root mean square error (RMSE) of 0.066 cm3.cm−3. This study provides an effective approach for soil moisture inversion on complex surfaces, simplifies the modeling process, and offers a tool for soil moisture monitoring across large spatial scales.

title: From Spectral Fidelity to LAI Identifiability: A PROSAIL–LESS–GEDI Assessment of Forest Overstory LAI Retrieval
summary: One-dimensional canopy radiative transfer models are widely used for leaf area index (LAI) retrieval, but their horizontally homogeneous representation can inadequately describe crown clumping, canopy gaps, woody elements, and shadowing in structurally complex forests. Explicit three-dimensional (3D) models offer greater structural realism, but their computational cost limits direct application at regional-to-continental scales. This study evaluates whether a residual correction distilled from the LargE-Scale remote sensing data and image simulation framework (LESS) 3.x into a PROSPECT + SAIL (PROSAIL) emulator improves forest overstory LAI identifiability when the inversion already has Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation (GEDI) relative-height metrics, canopy cover, and vertical-shape descriptors. The high-fidelity simulation library contains 3980 LESS scenes with explicit crowns and trunks (excluding understory and branches). Recomputing PROSAIL at the same Sentinel-2 band-center wavelengths yields a near-infrared 1D–3D reflectance residual of about −0.17, confirming a substantial structural discrepancy not attributable to spectral-response-function mismatch. On a structure-blocked split (2699 training and 1281 held-out validation scenes), with GEDI plant area index (PAI) excluded, the 1D inversion (E2) and multi-fidelity inversion (E5) use identical three-member ensembles and achieve LAI root-mean-square errors (RMSEs) of 1.564 and 1.563, respectively (R2 = 0.52). Block-bootstrap equivalence analysis yields a median ΔRMSE of −0.0009 with a 95% confidence interval of [−0.0025, −0.0001], entirely within the pre-specified ±0.05 LAI equivalence margin. The 3D residual reduces inverse spectral reconstruction RMSE from 0.038 to 0.034, but does not produce a practically meaningful LAI gain. An auxiliary joint LAI–clumping experiment is not identifiable (clumping R2 = −2.08), supporting treatment of clumping as a diagnostic rather than a retrieved product. Independent validation against Ground-Based Observations for Validation (GBOV) RM-7 Warren overstory LAI (187 observations, 16 sites) gives R2 = 0.30, r = 0.63, RMSE = 1.36, and bias = +0.16. These results show that improved 3D forward-model fidelity does not necessarily improve parameter identifiability when independent structural constraints are already present.

title: DMFNet: Phase-Enhanced Multi-Level Deformable Fusion for Multimodal Remote Sensing Classification
summary: The collaborative classification of hyperspectral images (HSI) with a complementary modality such as light detection and ranging (LiDAR) or synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which is known as multi-source remote sensing image classification (MRSIC), can combine rich spectral information with structural cues and is helpful for the recognition of complex ground objects.
