title: A Metro-InSAR Risk Index for corridor-scale displacement risk diagnosis of urban rail infrastructure
summary: Time-series Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) provides dense displacement observations along urban rail corridors, yet converting point-based measurements into corridor-scale diagnostic information remains challenging. This study proposes the Metro-InSAR Risk Index (MIRI), a diagnostic index designed to convert multi-dimensional InSAR-derived displacement characteristics into displacement-related diagnostic levels for urban metro corridors. MIRI integrates displacement rate, cumulative displacement, local displacement heterogeneity, height-related variability, and temporal residual variability, thereby extending conventional velocity-based interpretation toward corridor-scale displacement-risk diagnosis. The framework was applied to the Kunming Metro Network using 198 descending Sentinel-1 images acquired from March 2018 to December 2024. The time-series InSAR results show that the network was generally stable, with line-of-sight (LOS) displacement rates mainly ranging from −6 to 3 mm/yr and 97.21% of coherent scatterers falling within the stable interval of −3 to 3 mm/yr. Localized displacement anomalies were mainly observed near line intersections, curved sections, construction-affected areas, and the Dianchi Lake shoreline. Based on MIRI, 78%, 17%, 4%, and 1% of valid points were classified as Levels D, C, B, and A, respectively, indicating a distribution dominated by lower diagnostic levels, with spatially confined Level-B and Level-A anomalies particularly along Lines 4 and 5 and in lakeside soft-ground areas. Multi-source contextual variables and XGBoost-SHAP analysis were further used to interpret the environmental, anthropogenic, operational, and displacement-gradient information associated with the MIRI-based diagnostic patterns. The results indicate that the spatial variation in MIRI is mainly associated with terrain-related conditions, corridor-scale displacement variation, metro operation, and urban development intensity. By deriving diagnostic levels directly from PSI-based displacement indicators, MIRI provides an InSAR-based screening tool for prioritizing displacement-related anomalies and supporting maintenance of urban rail transit systems.

title: Deep learning detection of submesoscale eddies from MODIS SST in the South China Sea
summary: Submesoscale eddies play crucial roles in oceanic energy cascades and material transport; however, their detection faces substantial challenges owing to inadequate spatial resolution in traditional satellite altimetric measurements. This research introduces Sub-Eddy-Net, an innovative deep learning approach utilizing an enhanced YOLOv8-SGAM architecture for identifying submesoscale eddy features within MODIS-derived sea surface temperature (SST) imagery across the South China Sea region. By exploiting SST data's advantageous temporal coverage and observational continuity relative to altimetric sensors, synthetic aperture radar, and ocean color products, the developed algorithm demonstrates detection precision of 0.968, successfully identifying 20,443 submesoscale eddies throughout 2015–2024. Results indicate cyclonic eddy prevalence exceeds anticyclonic occurrences, exhibiting average radii of 13.1 km and 13.7 km respectively. Eddy distributions primarily cluster within coastal waters and Luzon Strait vicinity, displaying pronounced seasonal patterns. Comparison with Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) observations shows 64.3% matched features, 27.1% positional offsets, and 8.6% detected only in SST. Within the same eddies, coherent chlorophyll-a (Chla) signatures were present in a smaller fraction, indicating that SST is the more robust tracer for systematic detection. This Sub-Eddy-Net methodology offers a scalable approach for examining submesoscale oceanic phenomena, providing a decadal inventory for further study of their roles in ocean circulation and vertical exchange.

title: A GeoAI framework for remote-sensing-driven traffic activity and emission intensity in a data-scarce megacity
summary: In rapidly expanding megacities across the Global South, a profound data scarcity paradox frequently prevents effective environmental monitoring and evidence driven urban planning. While severe traffic congestion generates acute localised pollution, the total absence of continuous municipal traffic counters, ubiquitous vehicle telemetry, and air quality monitoring networks leaves these environments empirically unmonitored. This study resolves this challenge by introducing a reproducible geocomputational framework designed to map microscale traffic activity and relative emission landscapes by fusing multisource geospatial data and deep learning workflows. Focusing on the unmonitored context of Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of the Congo, our methodology uses very high resolution 15 cm satellite imagery to train and deploy a localised YOLOv8 (You Only Look Once, version 8) computer vision model, establishing an empirical baseline of fleet distribution. These static counts are dynamically distributed across the urban road network using a probabilistic Hub and Spoke Gravity Model, which is weighted through a zero shot Large Language Model semantic reclassification of unstructured OpenStreetMap features. Reconstructed kinematic flows are subsequently processed through velocity dependent Tier 3 EMEP/EEA algorithms to capture the nonlinear emission penalties triggered by severe network gridlock. To ensure framework defensibility, an independent unmanned aerial vehicle observation campaign was executed across ten distinct urban sites. The drone data directly validate model estimated physical parameters, achieving robust correlations for traffic volumes (R2 = 0.826) and link speeds (R2 = 0.925). Because literature derived chemical emission factors cannot be validated in situ, all absolute outputs are subjected to a rigorous multiparameter sensitivity analysis to report findings strictly as bounded ranges. The results reveal a clear structural handover in the spatial activity profile of the city. Daytime pollution is heavily driven by the informal paratransit fleet, which accounts for a bounded range of 82.8% to 95.1% of total PM2.5 emissions along primary corridors despite representing a numerical minority of active vehicles. Conversely, nocturnal baseline emissions transition to a landscape dominated almost entirely by private passenger vehicles. All code, processing pipelines, and validation datasets are available in a FAIR compliant open access repository. This framework establishes a scalable, remote sensing driven blueprint for diagnosing traffic activity structures in unmonitored metropolitan regions worldwide.

title: Transforming Leaf-Off LiDAR to leaf-on canopy height models using deep learning
summary: Accurate tree canopy metrics are essential for a wide range of ecological, environmental, and climate studies. Recent advances in airborne LiDAR sensing have greatly expanded access to high-resolution three-dimensional observations of tree canopy structure. However, many widely available airborne LiDAR datasets are acquired under leaf-off conditions to support terrain mapping, and our analysis across ecologically diverse sites shows that canopy height models (CHMs) derived from these data exhibit substantial, recurring discrepancies in canopy height and extent, with an overall tendency to underrepresent canopy structure relative to leaf-on conditions. These discrepancies limit the direct use of leaf-off CHMs in applications requiring canopy information representative of leaf-on conditions. To address this limitation, we introduce a deep learning framework for reconstructing leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs. To our knowledge, this is the first study to formulate the direct reconstruction of leaf-on CHMs from existing leaf-off LiDAR-derived CHMs as a supervised image-to-image learning task. The framework provides two complementary models: a Pix2Pix model that uses the leaf-off CHM alone and a U-Net model that additionally incorporates multispectral imagery. Our proposed models achieve robust canopy-height accuracy across four spatially independent test sites (R²: 0.85–0.92; Mean Absolute Error: 1.3–1.6 metres), substantially reducing the discrepancies observed in the leaf-off source CHMs. They also provide sharper delineation of canopy details and higher accuracy than recent optical-imagery-based approaches. To facilitate broader use, we developed an open-access web application that deploys the pre-trained models and supports on-demand leaf-on CHM generation for user-selected areas across the U.S. where suitable leaf-off LiDAR inputs are available. Overall, the framework provides a practical means to bridge the seasonal data gap in LiDAR acquisition and improve access to reliable canopy metrics representative of leaf-on conditions.

title: Second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling for spatial prediction
summary: Spatial prediction is a fundamental task in geographic information science and environmental resource assessment. However, under complex terrain and heterogeneous covariates, models relying only on point-scale attributes or a single global relationship often have difficulty representing spatial context and regional heterogeneity. This study proposes a second-dimension-enhanced spatial context-aware modeling framework (SDA-SCA) that integrates first-dimension covariates, neighborhood-based second-dimension features, covariate screening, spatially constrained stratification, and local model training. Using two independently constructed annual spatial-prediction cases based on surface solar radiation observations from 670 stations in China in 2022 and 2023, five modeling schemes—Ordinary Kriging, Geographically Weighted Random Forest (GWRF), first-dimension attribute modeling (FDA), second-dimension augmented modeling (SDA), and SDA-SCA—were evaluated under spatial cross-validation. SDA-SCA showed a consistent predictive advantage across the two independent annual cases and the three evaluated model families. Relative to FDA, SDA-SCA increased R2 by 0.11–0.16 in 2022 and 0.17–0.21 in 2023, while reducing RMSE by 12.4%–17.7% and 24.3%–33.7%, and MAE by 22.8%–35.5% and 31.5%–50.4%, respectively. Stage-wise ablation showed that the FDA-to-SDA step produced consistent but moderate improvements, whereas the SDA-to-SDA-SCA step provided larger and more stable gains. These results indicate that second-dimension features improve the representation of neighborhood context, and their predictive value is further strengthened when coupled with spatial stratification. SHAP analysis further confirmed the substantial contribution of second-dimension features to the integrated model. The proposed framework provides an extensible pathway for spatial prediction tasks requiring the joint representation of local attributes, neighborhood context, and spatial heterogeneity.
